title: Finding a Deceased Loved One's Money in Colorado (November 2026)
summary: This November 2026 guide explains Colorado unclaimed property searches, claim requirements, and how heirs can recover owed funds.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement in Colorado, families may find that the State Treasury holds unclaimed money or property that belonged to the person who died. Whether a claim is paid depends on the claimant's relationship to the person who died and on documents that prove ownership or heirship. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: how to search Colorado unclaimed property by name, what types of property the state holds, who is authorized to file a claim, what documents are required, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Families can search Colorado unclaimed property for free using a loved one's name.
- Colorado holds unclaimed assets indefinitely. Direct claims have no fee or filing deadline.
- Heir claims require proof of ownership or heirship; a matching name alone is not enough.
- Colorado searches exclude other states and accounts still held by banks or insurers.
- With IRS authorization, Elayne requests 10 years of tax transcripts to identify asset leads.


## What Is Unclaimed Property in Colorado?


Colorado unclaimed property is money or other assets transferred to the State Treasury when companies cannot locate owners for a legally defined period. The state's unclaimed property overview explains the basics. The Treasury holds property indefinitely for its owner or rightful heir until a valid claim is made.


Colorado’s Revised Uniform Unclaimed Property Act took effect in July 2020. An earlier legislative proposal describes when property is presumed abandoned.


In 2025, HB25-1224 changed virtual currency abandonment and transfer rules. For families, unclaimed assets can still be claimed after an owner dies.

## What Types of Property End Up with the State


Colorado unclaimed property reporting covers bank balances, insurance proceeds, and the Treasury’s other listed property types shown below. Banks, insurers, employers, and other businesses identify unclaimed property using the legal abandonment rules for each property type. Once those conditions are met and required owner-contact efforts are completed, they report the property and transfer it to the Treasury according to state requirements.


Money owed Other property


Uncashed checks and unpaid wages Stocks


Utility refunds and dividends Safe deposit box contents


After a death, these categories can help families[locate unclaimed property](https://www.elayne.com/resources/locating-unclaimed-property-parent) beyond checking and savings accounts.


The dormancy period is the time without owner activity before property is presumed abandoned.


- Most financial accounts have a three-year period.
- Under HB25-1224, virtual currency is presumed abandoned three years after the owner’s latest indication of interest.


Timing depends on property type.


## The Great Colorado Payback: Colorado's Unclaimed Property Program


The Great Colorado Payback is the Colorado Department of the Treasury’s unclaimed property program. Individuals, businesses, and nonprofits can claim lost assets with no filing time limit.


Measure Reported amount


Fiscal year 2026 returns Approximately $158 million; nearly 163,000 claims


April 2025 holdings Over $2 billion; more than 15 million individuals and entities


Average claim last year Approximately $918 ([Colorado Treasury](https://treasury.colorado.gov/payback) )


Individual claims can differ from the reported average.


## How to Search Colorado Unclaimed Property by Name


A free Colorado unclaimed property search begins with the name of the person who died.


1. The person's first and last name start the search. Former names, initials, and common misspellings can reveal other possible matches.
2. Past residences help narrow results, as the Treasury's search instructions explain.
3. Selected properties show the owner's name, city, ZIP code, reporting company, property ID, and amount in the claimed properties list.


A matching name is a lead, not proof. Colorado requires evidence of ownership or heirship before payment, which reflects broader standards covered in this[unclaimed inheritance search guide](https://www.elayne.com/resources/unclaimed-property-and-inheritance-search-guide) .


## Searching Beyond Colorado: Multi-State and National Searches


Each state maintains its own unclaimed property database. A Colorado unclaimed property search will not cover money held elsewhere for a loved one who died.


MissingMoney.com offers a free way to search multiple participating states. It is endorsed by the National Association of Unclaimed Property Administrators (NAUPA) and the National Association of State Treasurers.


For states outside that database, NAUPA’s[directory of state programs](https://unclaimed.org/search/) links to official websites for free searches. Searches can include every state where the person lived, did business, or held accounts.


## Who Is Authorized to Claim on Behalf of a Deceased Person


Colorado’s claimant relationship definitions identify “Heir/Estate Representative” as a qualifying sole rightful heir or legal estate representative. “Owner/Self” applies to the named owner. After a death, claimants identify their relationship to the person listed.


The[claim documentation requirements](https://unclaimedproperty.colorado.gov/app/claim/how-to-complete) include:


- An original signed claim form, sometimes requiring notarization.
- A copy of government-issued photo ID and a Social Security number.
- Evidence of ownership or heirship.


The claim email specifies which documents apply, and further evidence may be requested. A shared or similar name alone does not authorize payment to an heir, a principle that also applies when[finding a deceased person's money in Florida](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-loved-ones-money-florida) .

## How Elayne Supports Families Searching for Assets After a Death


Elayne Asset Search helps families build an estate inventory that goes beyond a Colorado unclaimed property search. The estate inventory lists the accounts, property, and debts that belonged to the person who died, and every entry names the source of the information.


Asset Search is used by the person responsible for settling the estate, most often an executor, spouse, or adult child who holds, or is about to hold, legal authority. Legal authority is the court document, such as letters testamentary or letters of administration, that lets a person act for the estate. Parts of the search can run before that document is issued, and the full search opens once legal authority is in place. Families stay in charge of the estate, and attorneys advise and file.


Colorado results and Asset Search results cover different records. The Great Colorado Payback lists property already transferred to the State Treasury. IRS tax transcripts and the Equifax credit report can point to accounts still held by banks, insurers, and employers.


With IRS authorization, Elayne requests 10 years of IRS tax transcripts for the person who died. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. A transcript lists what banks, brokerages, insurers, employers, and retirement account custodians reported to the IRS about the person, which can point to accounts that no statement or letter mentions. These reports include retirement distributions relevant to[finding unclaimed retirement benefits](https://www.elayne.com/resources/find-lost-retirement-accounts) .


Elayne also requests the person's Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, credit cards, and debts in the person's name. Other sources are checked in the same search:


- The NAIC life insurance policy locator, which covers in-force and lapsed policies, and MIB records of insurance applications.
- The PBGC pension registry, which lists unclaimed pensions from terminated plans.
- MissingMoney.com and state unclaimed property searches, which cover property turned over to the state.
- National property records and DMV records, which show real estate and vehicles titled in the person's name.
- Crypto exchange accounts and veterans benefits, which are searched when the estate record points to crypto holdings or veteran status.


Each finding is added to the estate inventory with the institution that reported the finding. Debts appear next to assets, and the search also shows whether the estate owes the IRS anything. A one-on-one call with an Estate Expert, available within 24 hours, walks through the findings.


Every family begins with a free start at no charge. Asset Search is priced at $3,000 in total, which includes Estate Setup. The fee is an eligible estate expense, paid from the estate account or reimbursed to a family member who advanced the payment. Based on internal case data, it's estimated that families using Elayne have located over $5 million in assets.


## FAQ


### Can heirs claim a loved one’s money through the Great Colorado Payback if they left no will?


Yes, a missing will does not prevent a claim, but claimants still need proof that they qualify as a rightful heir or legal estate representative. The Great Colorado Payback’s claim email lists the required evidence; an estate attorney can clarify who may claim when inheritance rights are uncertain.


### What does it mean if the Great Colorado Payback and MissingMoney.com show no results shortly after a death?


The person’s statements, mail, and insurance paperwork can identify institutions for families to contact directly. A Colorado unclaimed property search with no results does not rule out assets: money may still be held by a bank or insurer and may not appear in state databases until years later.


### How is a Great Colorado Payback claim handled when the deceased person has multiple heirs?


When several people share inheritance rights, no individual heir is the sole rightful heir. Claimants identify their actual relationship to the deceased owner and provide the evidence Colorado requests. When an estate representative is handling the claim, keeping the property ID, submitted documents, and payment records in the estate’s shared records helps heirs follow the process; the estate’s attorney can advise to ensure everything is handled correctly.


### Is there a fee or a deadline to claim a deceased person’s property from the Great Colorado Payback?


Direct claims filed with the Colorado State Treasury have no fee and no filing deadline. The Treasury holds unclaimed property indefinitely for the owner or rightful heir until a valid claim is made. Unclaimed assets can still be claimed after the owner dies.
